subject: Art & Design
title: The Invention of New Pigments
description: A micro-lesson that makes The Invention of New Pigments usable.

hook.text: For centuries, blue was rarer than gold. Then a German pharmacist accidentally invented Prussian blue.

buildup.text: Ancient artists had very few pigments. Ultramarine came from grinding lapis lazuli — semi-precious stone.

discovery.text: The 19th century's synthetic pigment revolution gave artists colors they'd never had access to.

twist.text: Some historic pigments were lethal. Scheele's Green contained arsenic and may have killed Napoleon.

climax.text: Today, scientists are still inventing pigments. YInMn Blue was discovered in 2009 by accident.

punchline.text: Every new pigment unlocked art that was previously impossible.

quiz.question: Why was blue historically one of the most expensive colors?
options: It required grinding semi-precious lapis lazuli stone
Blue light is harder to see

details.summary: Throughout history, new pigments have transformed art — Egyptian blue (3000 BCE), ultramarine from lapis lazuli, cadmium yellow, and synthetic pigments that replaced toxic lead and arsenic colors. YInMn Blue, discovered accidentally in 2009, was the first new blue pigment in over 200 years.
details.whyItMatters: Available pigments directly shaped art history — the Pre-Raphaelites painted differently than the Impressionists partly because new pigments became available.
takeaways: New pigments have transformed art throughout history
YInMn Blue was the first new blue in over 200 years, discovered in 2009
Material science directly drives creative possibilities in art

faq.question: What is YInMn Blue? — more details inside the topic.
faq.answer: Discovered in 2009 by Mas Subramanian at Oregon State University while researching electronics materials. It's made from yttrium, indium, and manganese oxides. It's remarkably stable, non-toxic, UV-reflective, and maintains its vivid blue in any condition — superior to many existing blue pigments.

faq.question: Were historical pigments really dangerous?
faq.answer: Many were lethal. Paris Green contained arsenic and was used in wallpaper — potentially contributing to Napoleon's death. Lead white caused painter's colic. Vermilion was mercury sulfide. Scheele's Green was arsenic-based. Modern synthetic pigments replaced most toxic historical colors.
